title: Critical Reading & Text Investigation
description: Analysing how writers create meaning — investigating language and structure in fiction and non-fiction, context, characterisation, setting, symbolism and theme.

notes.heading: What Analysis Is — and the Four-Step Method

illustration.alt: Flow diagram of the four-step analysis method — identify the technique, answer the question, explain the effect on the reader, explore the writer's intention — with a worked example using the simile 'solitary as an oyster'.
illustration.caption: Build every analytical paragraph in four steps: identify the technique, answer the question, explain the effect, explore the writer's intention.

notes.body: Comprehension tells you WHAT a text says; analysis tells you HOW it works. To analyse, zoom in on a short, interesting section and ask three questions: what has the writer done, what effect does it create, and why might the writer have wanted that effect? Build every analytical paragraph in four steps: (1) Identify the technique — name what the writer has done ('the writer uses a simile'). (2) Answer the question in one sentence — link the technique to the point you're making ('to present the teacher as tense and unpredictable'). (3) Explain the effect on the reader — 'stormy' suggests his mood could break at any moment, so we sympathise with the pupils. (4) Explore the writer's intention — what bigger idea or later event does this moment set up? Push for layers: one image can carry several meanings ('solitary as an oyster' — shut tight against people, but also only emerging to feed, so only sociable when it pays). A practical obstacle to close reading is unfamiliar vocabulary. You don't need a dictionary for every word: read around the word for context clues, break it into prefix/root/suffix ('incredulous' = in- 'not' + cred 'believe'), work out its word class from the sentence, and decide whether you even need it — you can follow a text comfortably knowing most, not all, of its words.

notes.heading: Investigating Language in Fiction
notes.body: Fiction writers choose every word deliberately, so treat word choice as evidence. Start with connotation — the feelings and associations a word carries beyond its dictionary meaning ('dismal' rain is sadder than 'heavy' rain). Look for imagery: similes and metaphors that smuggle in extra meaning, and personification that makes a setting feel alive or threatening ('the house seemed to watch her'). Listen to sound: alliteration draws attention to a phrase; sibilance (repeated 's' sounds) can hiss with menace. Notice perspective markers — pronouns like 'I' and 'my' pull the reader inside a narrator's head. Watch for foreshadowing: small details (a candle nearly burnt out, a door left unlocked) that hint at what is coming. Pitfall: don't just technique-spot. 'The writer uses a simile' earns nothing until you explain what the comparison suggests and how it shapes the reader's response. Always travel the full chain: technique → effect → meaning.

notes.heading: Investigating Language in Non-Fiction
notes.body: Non-fiction writers are usually trying to DO something to the reader — persuade, shock, reassure, amuse, advise — so language analysis here means asking how the words push you towards a reaction. Key things to investigate: emotive language ('helpless animals', 'reckless drivers') that tells you what to feel; direct address and personal pronouns ('you', 'we') that make the issue feel like your business; register — formal vocabulary for authority, informal for friendliness; and patterns of emphasis such as repetition or triads ('these animals are suffering, starving and silent') that make an idea stick. Also notice what is left out: which facts are selected, and whose voice is missing. This builds directly on the bias and loaded-language work from Reading Comprehension — but now you go beyond spotting that a text is one-sided to explaining how each choice (a statistic here, an anecdote there, a headline word) constructs that effect. The same techniques work in reverse: analysing how others influence readers teaches you to use these tools in your own writing.

notes.heading: Investigating Structure in Fiction and Non-Fiction
notes.body: Structure is the order and arrangement of a text — and order creates meaning. In fiction, investigate: narrative perspective (who tells the story controls what we know and how we judge); syntax — the arrangement of words in a sentence ('Marley was dead, to begin with' wrong-foots the reader with its final phrase); sentence and paragraph length — short sentences and one-line paragraphs create tension and dramatic impact, long ones build atmosphere or confusion; dialogue and internal monologue, which reveal what characters say versus what they privately think; and the relationship between openings and endings — a story that closes with an echo of its opening image (endings becoming new beginnings) has been deliberately shaped. In non-fiction, investigate: word order — fronting a word gives it force ('Appallingly, many factories still use child labour' hits harder than burying 'appalling' mid-sentence); punctuation — a question mark makes a line reflective, an exclamation mark frustrated, an ellipsis uncertain; and repetition of key words to drum in a message. Ask of every structural choice: how would the text feel different if it were ordered another way?

notes.heading: Characterisation and Setting
notes.body: Characterisation is how a writer builds a person on the page. Writers work through many tools at once: physical description, but also movement and voice; actions and habits; dialogue — what a character says and how they say it; names (a character called 'Squealer' carries a hint of betrayal); and the opinions of other characters ('he could turn black into white'). Track the character's arc — how they change, or pointedly refuse to change — and notice archetypes: stock figures like the hero, villain, outsider or trickster that a writer can use straight or deliberately subvert. Setting is equally deliberate. It fixes time and place, but also: creates atmosphere (an isolated, wind-battered house feels tense before anything happens); establishes genre (a crumbling castle tells you what kind of story you're in); reveals character (the tidy door for the respectable self, the sinister back door for the hidden one); and reflects theme (a divided city embodying prejudice). Test your reading by swapping the setting — the same story on a sunny beach would collapse — which proves the setting was doing real work.

notes.heading: Symbolism and Themes
notes.body: A symbol is a concrete thing — an object, place, colour, weather — that stands for an abstract idea: a heart for love, a dove for peace, a fork in the road for a life choice. Symbols work through connotation, so their meaning depends on context: red means stop at a traffic light, danger in a thriller, passion in a love poem. Writers use symbols to deepen atmosphere, hint at character, or comment on life, and a symbol repeated across a text becomes a motif that ties the work together. Theme is the big idea the text is really about — distinct from plot, which is simply what happens. The plot of a novel might be 'a boy discovers he is a wizard'; its themes are good versus evil and the power of friendship. Themes are usually universal (ambition, prejudice, grief, appearance versus reality), which is why texts written centuries and continents apart can share them. To find themes, look for repeated images, ideas and contrasts. One caution: don't over-read. A symbol must earn its interpretation from the context of the story — sometimes a tree really is just a tree.

notes.heading: Context, Effect on the Reader — Applied: Gothic Literature
notes.body: No text is written in a vacuum. Context is the world around the writing: social (how people lived and believed), historical (what was happening at the time), political (power, war, censorship), biographical (the writer's own life) and literary (the genres and styles fashionable at the time). Context also covers reading: a contemporary reader in 1818 met Frankenstein in a world without electric light, so animating a creature with a 'spark' felt astonishingly new; a modern reader brings CCTV and AI to the same pages. Effect on the reader is the goal of every technique in this topic — the mood a writer builds and the feelings it triggers — and you can discuss effects on yourself, on readers in general, on specific groups, and on contemporary versus modern audiences. Apply it all to the Gothic genre: its conventions are isolated, decaying settings (moors, ruined castles) that trap characters; night and storm that tap our instinctive fear of the dark; supernatural or uncanny characters contrasting victim and predator, good and evil; themes of transgression, revenge and science overreaching; and symbolic omens (a full moon, a raven) foreshadowing disaster. When you can explain how setting, character, symbol and structure combine to produce a shiver, you are doing full critical reading.

flashcards.definition: Explaining how a text works — identifying a writer's choices and exploring their effect and purpose, rather than just what the text says.
flashcards.example: Not 'Scrooge is mean' but 'Dickens compares Scrooge to an oyster to suggest he has sealed himself off from human contact.'

flashcards.definition: The feelings and associations a word carries beyond its literal dictionary meaning (its denotation).
flashcards.example: 'Home' denotes a place you live; it connotes warmth, safety and belonging.

flashcards.definition: Repetition of soft 's' and 'sh' sounds, often used to create a sinister, whispering or soothing mood.
flashcards.example: 'The snake slid silently through the grass' — the hissing sounds mirror the danger.

flashcards.definition: Hints or clues planted early in a text that suggest events still to come.
flashcards.example: A candle 'nearly burnt out' just as a creature opens its eyes hints that darkness and death will follow.

flashcards.definition: The point of view from which a story is told; first person ('I') puts readers inside the narrator's head, learning as they learn.
flashcards.example: Pronouns like 'I' and 'me' signal first person, so we experience events exactly as the character does.

flashcards.definition: The arrangement of words and phrases in a sentence; changing the order changes the emphasis and effect.
flashcards.example: 'Appallingly, many factories still use child labour' fronts the judgement word for maximum impact.

flashcards.definition: A character's private thoughts presented directly to the reader, revealing feelings and conflicts that dialogue hides.
flashcards.example: A character politely answers a guard's questions while their italicised thoughts give the sarcastic replies they dare not say aloud.

flashcards.definition: The methods a writer uses to build a character — appearance, actions, dialogue, names, movement, and other characters' opinions.
flashcards.example: Describing how a character skips and twitches while arguing makes him feel untrustworthy before he does anything wrong.

flashcards.definition: The mood of a text — how it feels to read — created mainly through setting and language choices.
flashcards.example: An isolated farmhouse battered by wind creates an atmosphere of tension and exposure.

flashcards.definition: A concrete object, place, colour or event that stands for an abstract idea; its meaning depends on context.
flashcards.example: A fork in the road can symbolise a life-changing choice; a dove symbolises peace.

flashcards.definition: The big idea a text is really about — a universal concept explored through the story, distinct from the plot.
flashcards.example: Plot: a man murders his king to take the throne. Themes: ambition, fate, appearance versus reality.

flashcards.definition: The circumstances in which a text is written and read — social, historical, political, biographical and literary — which shape its meanings.
flashcards.example: A novel about total surveillance read very differently in 1949 than it does to a reader surrounded by CCTV today.

questions.stem: A student wants to analyse a paragraph rather than just summarise it. What should their FIRST step be?
choices: Identify what the writer has done — find a specific language or structural choice to focus on
Write a personal opinion about whether the text is enjoyable
Look up the writer's biography for context
Count how many similes the paragraph contains
questions.explanation: Analysis begins with close observation: zoom into a short section and identify a concrete choice the writer has made (a word, image, sentence shape). Only then can you explain its effect and the writer's intention. Opinion and context come later in the chain, and simply counting techniques is technique-spotting, not analysis.

choices: The dictionary definition of a word
The number of syllables in a word
A word's origin in another language
The feelings and associations a word suggests beyond its literal meaning
questions.explanation: Connotation is the layer of suggested meaning around a word — 'slim' and 'skinny' denote the same thing but connote very differently. The dictionary definition is the denotation; word origins are etymology. Writers exploit connotations to steer a reader's feelings.

questions.stem: 'He kept his thoughts locked away, solitary as an oyster.' The underlined phrase is an example of:
choices: A metaphor
A simile
Alliteration
Foreshadowing
questions.explanation: A simile compares two things using 'like' or 'as' — here 'solitary as an oyster'. A metaphor would state he IS an oyster. The comparison lets the reader import the oyster's qualities: a hard shell shut against the world, opening only when it gains something.

questions.stem: A writer ends a tense chapter with three one-sentence paragraphs. The most likely intended effect is:
choices: To slow the pace and let the reader relax
To save space on the page
To create dramatic impact and make each moment land sharply
To show that the narrator has nothing left to say
questions.explanation: Short sentences and one-line paragraphs are a structural tool: they speed up the reading rhythm, isolate each statement, and heighten shock or tension — the opposite of relaxation. Structure is deliberate, so 'saving space' mistakes accident for craft, and brevity here signals intensity, not emptiness.

questions.stem: A story is narrated entirely in the first person ('I sat up. The dog was dead.'). What does this perspective chiefly give the reader?
choices: A guarantee that the narrator is telling the complete truth
Events experienced through the character's eyes, learning information only as they do
Knowledge of what every character is thinking
An objective, detached view of the events
questions.explanation: First person confines us inside one consciousness: we see what they see, when they see it, filtered through their personality. That is exactly why it cannot be objective (third-person omniscient would give access to all minds), and it does not guarantee honesty — narrators can be biased or unreliable.

questions.stem: A writer introduces a character: 'a small fat man with twinkling eyes, nimble movements and a shrill voice; the others said he could talk anyone into anything.' Which characterisation tools are being combined?
choices: Only physical appearance
Setting and symbolism
Appearance, movement, voice, and other characters' opinions
Internal monologue and foreshadowing
questions.explanation: Characterisation layers several tools: looks ('small fat'), how he moves ('nimble'), how he sounds ('shrill') and what others say about him ('could talk anyone into anything') — together building an impression of persuasive slipperiness. No setting or symbol is present, and we never hear his private thoughts.

questions.stem: A novel opens in 'a farmhouse standing alone on a wind-battered moor, miles from the nearest road.' Beyond fixing time and place, what is this setting chiefly doing?
choices: Providing comic relief
Showing the author likes the countryside
Establishing that the story is non-fiction
Creating an atmosphere of isolation and vulnerability, where help cannot easily arrive
questions.explanation: Setting is a deliberate tool: isolation plus hostile weather builds atmosphere and signals that characters are exposed and escape is hard — a hallmark of Gothic-influenced fiction. Setting can also reflect theme and character. Nothing here suggests comedy, the author's hobbies, or non-fiction.

questions.stem: Four students interpret a poem in which a tree appears beside a front door in every stanza. Whose reading shows the strongest grasp of symbolism?
choices: A: 'The tree is a symbol — every tree in every poem always means nature.'
B: 'The tree is definitely the poet's code for her bank account.'
C: 'Trees are not symbols, so the tree adds nothing to the poem.'
D: 'The tree is repeated and outlasts each visitor at the door, so in this poem it may symbolise endurance — though I'd check the context before pushing further.'
questions.explanation: Good symbolic reading is anchored in the specific text: repetition (a motif) plus context justifies the reading of endurance, and the caution against over-reading shows real judgement. A applies a fixed universal meaning regardless of context; B asserts a link with no textual evidence; C wrongly rules out symbolism altogether.

questions.stem: Which of these is a THEME rather than a plot point?
choices: The hero travels across the desert to find his sister
The corrupt mayor is finally arrested in the last chapter
The novel argues that appearances can deceive — charm often hides cruelty
Two brothers argue about money at their father's funeral
questions.explanation: A theme is the big idea the story explores — appearance versus reality is a universal concept the whole text can argue. The other options are events: things that happen. Plot is what happens; theme is what the story is really about beneath the surface.

questions.stem: A playwright writes a ghost story partly because ghost stories are fashionable in the theatres of her day and audiences expect one. Which kind of context best explains this influence?
choices: Literary context
Biographical context
Political context
Historical context
questions.explanation: Literary context covers the genres, styles and works surrounding a writer — what other writers are producing and what is popular. Biographical context would be events from her own life; political and historical context concern governments and world events, not theatrical fashion.

questions.stem: Compare: 'Appallingly, many factories still use child labour' vs 'Many factories still use child labour, which is appalling.' Why is the first version more forceful?
choices: It is longer, so it carries more information
Fronting 'Appallingly' makes the writer's judgement hit the reader before the facts arrive
It uses a rhetorical question to involve the reader
It avoids emotive language, making it more objective
questions.explanation: Word order (syntax) controls emphasis: opening with the emotive adverb frames everything that follows as an outrage, so the reader absorbs the facts through the writer's judgement. The second version makes the judgement an afterthought. The sentence is not a question, and 'Appallingly' is the opposite of objective.

questions.stem: 'Will our society ever solve this problem…' Ending the sentence with an ellipsis rather than a question mark changes the effect to:
choices: Anger and frustration
Excitement and urgency
Uncertainty — the thought trails off, as if the answer may never come
No change — punctuation never affects meaning
questions.explanation: Punctuation shapes tone: a question mark would make the line reflective, an exclamation mark frustrated or urgent, while the ellipsis lets the sentence fade, suggesting doubt and an unresolved future. Claiming punctuation never affects meaning ignores a structural tool writers use constantly.

questions.stem: Which opening most clearly signals that a story belongs to the Gothic genre?
choices: On a bright June morning, friends gathered on the beach to plan the school fair
The detective reviewed the witness statements over a strong coffee at headquarters
Beyond the ruined abbey, the storm split the sky; somewhere in its empty corridors a door slammed, though no living soul had entered for a century
Mina checked her phone: the train was delayed again, and she was going to miss the match
questions.explanation: Gothic conventions cluster here: an isolated, decaying setting (ruined abbey), a storm and darkness tapping fear of the night, and a supernatural or uncanny hint (the self-slamming door) foreshadowing danger. The sunny beach, the routine police work and the delayed train all belong to other genres and moods.

questions.stem: You meet the word 'incredulous' in a sentence: 'Dana gave me an incredulous look — she clearly didn't believe a word of it.' What is the BEST first strategy?
choices: Stop reading immediately and memorise a dictionary definition
Use the surrounding context — 'didn't believe a word of it' reveals the meaning
Skip the sentence entirely and hope the word doesn't matter
Assume it means the same as 'incredible' in the sense of amazing
questions.explanation: Context clues are the fastest tool: the second half of the sentence restates the word's meaning (disbelieving). Word parts help too (in- 'not' + cred 'believe'). Stopping for a dictionary breaks your flow as a first resort, skipping loses information, and guessing from a lookalike word produces the wrong meaning.

questions.stem: A story begins: 'The fog came down at dusk and swallowed the streetlamps one by one.' Which analytical comment explores the language most fully?
choices: The writer uses fog to show that the weather is foggy
The writer personifies the fog — it 'swallows' the lights like a predator — so the setting seems alive and threatening, and the disappearing lamps foreshadow a loss of safety
The writer uses long words to confuse the reader
The writer mentions streetlamps because the characters need light to see
questions.explanation: The strongest comment completes the analytical chain: it names the technique (personification), explores connotations ('swallowed' = predator, consumption), links to effect (threat) and intention (foreshadowing danger). The other options restate the literal surface or invent motives with no textual basis — technique-spotting without meaning.
